title: The Shell Is a Programming Language

questions.q: When you run 'ls *.txt' on your Pi and it matches several files, what does the 'ls' program actually receive as its arguments?
choices: The literal string '*.txt', which ls expands itself
The final list of matching filenames, already expanded by the shell
Nothing — ls reads the current directory on its own and ignores the pattern
A special wildcard token that ls knows how to interpret
questions.explain: Globbing is done by the shell before the program runs, so ls is handed the finished filename list and never sees the '*'. ls has no idea a wildcard was ever typed. The literal '*.txt' is only passed when nothing matches (the default no-match behavior).

questions.q: A variable holds 'my report.txt'. Why does 'rm $file' fail but 'rm "$file"' work?
choices: Unquoted, the value is word-split on the space into two arguments; quoting suppresses the splitting so rm gets one filename
The dollar sign must always be escaped, and only double quotes do that
rm cannot handle file extensions unless the variable is quoted
Single quotes would be required instead; double quotes make no difference here
questions.explain: Unquoted expansions are split on IFS, so 'my report.txt' becomes two words ('my' and 'report.txt'). Double quotes suppress word splitting so rm receives the single real filename. The dollar sign expands fine either way — the problem is splitting, not escaping.

choices: cd is an external program found via PATH, like ls
cd must be a shell builtin, because a child process cannot change its parent's working directory
cd works only in login shells, not in scripts
cd is an alias that bash rewrites into 'pushd'
questions.explain: An external program runs in a child process, and a child cannot alter its parent's directory — so cd must run inside the shell itself as a builtin. The same necessity applies to export, read, pwd, and '['.

questions.q: The guide calls 'which' a myth for finding commands. Why, and what should you use instead?
choices: which is slow; use 'locate' instead for speed
which is an external program blind to builtins, functions, and aliases, so it lies about things like cd and ll — use 'type -a'
which only works as root; use 'sudo which' instead
which is correct, but 'type -a' is just a shorter alias for it
questions.explain: which is an external program with no knowledge of the shell's builtins, functions, or aliases, so it misreports things like cd. 'type -a' is shell-aware and reports what would truly run, including its kind and location.

questions.q: An alias and a custom PATH entry work fine in your terminal but a cron job can't find them. What's the usual cause?
choices: Cron has a bug that strips environment variables at random
Cron runs non-interactive and non-login, so it reads neither ~/.bashrc nor ~/.bash_profile and your customizations don't exist there
The alias was defined with single quotes, which cron cannot parse
Cron always runs as root, which has a separate PATH you forgot to edit
questions.explain: Cron jobs run non-interactive and non-login with a minimal environment, reading neither ~/.bashrc (interactive) nor the login startup files — so aliases and PATH tweaks defined there simply aren't present. The fix is to source what you need explicitly rather than assume your interactive environment exists.
